messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: A first draft of a transition guide from ggplot-0.8.9 to 0.9.0: RFC
parts:
Greetings:

Attached is a first draft of what is intended to be a transition guide
for ggplot2 users moving from 0.8.9 to 0.9.0. I'd like to ask you to
look it over and provide feedback to me about things that are missing
or could be improved either in the examples or text. Most of the new
geoms are illustrated as well as the guide functions, but I'm sure
I'm missing things that could improve the document in a number of
ways. Organizational tips are welcome, too. The goal is to try to get
the average user of ggplot2 up to speed more quickly with respect to
the current changes and additions in the package.

I've deliberately omitted providing examples of the new stat_
functions, but it would be useful to include more examples where the
code in 0.8.9 does not work in 0.9.0 and what the replacement code
would be. I envisioned that as a separate section of the document, to
be 'rbinded' to the current version.

This document was produced with the new knitr package developed by
Yihui Xie from Iowa State. I thank him for his help on the several
occasions I've bothered him today about different aspects of the code.
If you like what you see, install the package from CRAN and go to its
website to learn more about it: http://yihui.github.com/knitr/

Several plots in this document were changed from pdf to png to reduce
the file size; if you print this and find a few of the graphs rather
grainy or pixillated, that's why. There are also three places in the
document where bugs in the current 0.9.0 are pointed out; I know that
two of them are reported and I'm sending a message about the third one
this evening just in case. Since bugs are usually fixed pretty
quickly, hopefully the correct output will be there soon.

Also note that this is a transition guide for experienced users of
ggplot2 and not an introductory tutorial. Feel free to reply through
the list or privately.

Dennis

messages.author: 69658a5d047f38b4
messages.subject: Re: A first draft of a transition guide from ggplot-0.8.9 to 0.9.0: RFC
parts:
Hi all,

Pre-scriptum: I've just made aware of the dev list by a post by Winston on the regular one and just subscribed. I was JiHO on the other list but decided that ggplot is close enough to "work" that I can use my real name now ;) It's great to see ggplot development picked up by many talented people in addition to Hadley. I never got to the point of submitting much code but hopefully I'll be able to continue to help with bug reports and the documentation.

Now regarding the document and changes in ggplot in general:

That's an incredible resource! And it shows me I haven't been using the development version of ggplot enough…

Congrats on the scales work which looks very powerful. But I wouldn't be me if I wasn't nitpicking: it's a lot of functions calling other functions, with some functions that can't be tested on their own (i.e. date_breaks("4 months") does not do anything on its own) and this makes it a bit harder to explain and learn, i.e. ideally, I'd like to be able to write

scale_x_date(breaks = "10 weeks")

rather than

scale_x_date(breaks = date_breaks("10 weeks"))

since the scale is a date scale, it seems like it would be possible to know that it needs to handle the "10 weeks" argument with date_breaks(). I understand that, from a programming point of view it makes sense to have the same argument take the same kind of data in every scale_* function. I'm just wondering if, in some cases, it would be possible to make it a bit easier for the user.

I love the new possibilities offered by guide_*(). Here again that's a lot of new functions called by functions though. From a user point of view, having a width and height argument to scale_* and use that as barwidth/height in guide_colourbar and keywidth/height in guide_legend, for example, would be a bit more abstracted and more natural. But maybe you intend guide() to become the main interface?
Any chance on having colourbar become the default for continuous scales?
Are there plans to integrate colourbars with other key-based legend to avoid having two legends in this case:

d=data.frame(x=runif(10), y=runif(10))
qplot(x, y, data=d, colour=x, size=x) + guides(colour=guide_colourbar())

I thought about something like this: http://dl.dropbox.com/u/1047321/ggplot/scale_gradient_ggplot2.pdf when we discussed it a while ago with Hadley.

The dotplot and violin geoms are great. I slapped together small functions to get those done before (e.g. https://gitorious.org/r/r-utils/blobs/master/lib_ggplot.R, at the very bottom) but could never make them into proper geoms. So thanks a lot, I'll be using those two often (particularly if geom_dotplot ends up working in polar coords!).
<nipicking mode> What is the reason to use while shapes with an outline as the default in geom_violin rather than dark grey shapes as with all other "filled" geoms (bars, polygon, ribbon etc.)? </nipicking mode> ;)

That's all details of course (but if the devil is in the details, perfection is also there!) so thanks a lot again.


As for the document itself, I found it mostly clear and well laid out. I would add a table of contents on the first page. I also had trouble copy-pasting from the example but I don't know if it is something you could fix.

My only remark is that I think you should keep the data generation part of the examples as simple as possible to focus people on the ggplot syntax. The maps examples are quite complex for example but short of pre-preparating the data and putting it online, you will have a hard time making it really simpler. But for the correlation matrix example you could probably generate it without the need for mutate() for example.
Related to that, you should probably include the library() calls in the examples. My version of melt does not produce Var1 and Var2 but X1 and X2 as column names so the mutate() call does not work. I guess you used a new version of reshape or reshape2 but I had no way to know.

The dotplot and violin geoms are great. I slapped together small functions to get those done before (e.g. https://gitorious.org/r/r-utils/blobs/master/lib_ggplot.R, at the very bottom) but could never make them into proper geoms. So thanks a lot, I'll be using those two often (particularly if geom_dotplot ends up working in polar coords!).
<nipicking mode> What is the reason to use while shapes with an outline as the default in geom_violin rather than dark grey shapes as with all other "filled" geoms (bars, polygon, ribbon etc.)? </nipicking mode> ;)

I can answer this one... there wasn't any particularly principled reason for itl. I based the geom_violin code on geom_boxplot, which has a white fill and black outline, and so geom_violin ended up with the same colors. I kind of like the white fill with the outline, but then, I've never really liked the default dark-grey fill. If it's to be changed, I guess now is the time to do it, before 0.9.0 is released -- I guess this is something for Hadley to decide?
